title: If you want peace
author: Vegetius
setting: A late Roman military handbook, late 4th or 5th century AD

edition.name: Vegetius, Epitoma rei militaris, book 3, Latin text as presented by The Latin Library (thelatinlibrary.com), headed "FLAVI VEGETI RENATI VIRI INLUSTRIS COMITIS EPITOMA REI MILITARIS LIBER III"; the page does not name the printed edition it reproduces
edition.section: Book 3, preface (unnumbered on the page), last two sentences

source_text: Igitur qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum; qui uictoriam cupit, milites inbuat diligenter; qui secundos optat euentus, dimicet arte, non casu. Nemo prouocare, nemo audet offendere quem intellegit superiorem esse, si pugnet.
excerpt_note: The last two sentences of the preface to Book 3, which comes before section I on the page. The Latin was taken from The Latin Library page (thelatinlibrary.com/vegetius3.html), which names no edition; it has not been checked against Lang's Teubner text (1885) or any other printed edition. The text prints u for consonantal v (uictoriam, euentus, prouocare) and inbuat for imbuat; both are kept as printed.

translation: So whoever wants peace should get ready for war; whoever longs for victory should train his soldiers thoroughly; whoever hopes for good results should fight by skill, not by luck. No one dares to challenge, no one dares to attack, a man he knows would come out on top in a fight.
translation_note: Three parallel commands, each "quī ... (he) who ..." with a jussive subjunctive (praeparet, inbuat, dīmicet), then the reason. In the last sentence the antecedent of quem is left out ("[him] whom"), and sī pugnet is a condition reported inside the indirect statement: "would be the stronger, if he were to fight".

essay.t: Flavius Vegetius Renatus wrote the Epitoma rei militaris, a short handbook urging Rome to revive the drilled infantry legion of earlier times.
Britannica calls him a reformer with little military experience of his own and dates the work to 384–389.

The date is disputed. Many scholars, among them the editor Carl Lang, place the work under Theodosius I, late in the fourth century; Gibbon and Otto Seeck (1876) preferred Valentinian III, in the fifth, and Walter Goffart argues for Valentinian III, building on a hint of Gibbon's.
Our sentences close the preface to Book 3.
Just before them he recalls that Hannibal, bound for Italy, hired a Spartan teacher of warfare.
The conclusion is a chain of three parallel commands followed by a reason: no one dares to provoke an opponent he knows would win.
The famous Latin form, si vis pacem, para bellum ("if you want peace, prepare for war"), is not what Vegetius wrote: his words are qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum.
I could not trace the short form to any classical author or find when it first appeared; it looks like a later condensation of this sentence, and its origin should be treated as unknown.
Even Britannica lists "If you want peace, prepare for war" among the work's aphorisms: true of the sense, not the wording.

The idea is older than Vegetius. In his seventh Philippic, against Mark Antony, Cicero told the senate that if they wished to enjoy peace they must wage war (si pace frui volumus, bellum gerendum est).
Cornelius Nepos has Epaminondas answer Meneclides, who was urging the Thebans to prefer peace, that peace is won by war (paritur pax bello).

Vegetius had little effect on the late Roman army, Britannica says, but became hugely influential in the Middle Ages and was long called "the military bible of Europe"; George Washington owned and annotated a copy.
A review of Marco Formisano's 2003 edition likewise notes the work's widespread medieval success and its reading by humanists.
The irony: his most quoted sentence is usually quoted in words he did not use.

questions.q: According to the essay, which earlier Roman said something similar in a speech against Mark Antony?
Why is the date of the work uncertain?
options: Scholars split between Theodosius I and Valentinian III
The only manuscript breaks off before the preface
Vegetius dates it by a consul no one can identify
It survives only in a medieval Greek translation
